name: Tragedy of the commons
scope: The tragedy-of-the-commons argument as William Forster Lloyd first stated it (1833) and Garrett Hardin made it a political doctrine in his 1968 Science essay: where a resource is open to all, each user gains fully from taking more while the cost is shared, so rational users ruin it, and the remedy lies in political and social arrangements (mutual coercion mutually agreed upon, privatisation or regulation, population control) rather than in technical fixes. The scope is that argument and its prescriptions as stated by Hardin's essay, his own later account (Econlib) and the reference works (Britannica, Gale Encyclopedia of Environmental Science). It excludes the critics' positions (Ostrom's account of self-governed commons, Dahlman's and Angus's historical objections), which only show that the argument is a set of ideas, and excludes the broader commons movement, eco-capitalism and laissez-faire.

keyFigures.role: Ecologist whose 1968 essay made the argument a doctrine of population control and mutual coercion over shared resources.
keyFigures.quote: The idea of the tragedy of the commons was made popular by the American ecologist Garrett Hardin

keyFigures.role: Oxford political economist whose 1833 common-pasture example the argument is built on.
keyFigures.quote: In 1832 William Forster Lloyd, a political economist at Oxford University

keyWorks.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
keyWorks.quote: Hardin, Garrett. “The Tragedy of the Commons.” Science 162 (1968): 1243–1248.

summary: The tragedy of the commons is the argument, from William Forster Lloyd and Garrett Hardin, that where a resource is open to all each user gains fully from taking more while the cost is shared, so rational users ruin it. Hardin concluded that there is no technical fix: users must accept mutual coercion mutually agreed upon (laws, taxes, enclosure or private property), and above all must give up the freedom to breed. Its sources record few positions beyond that, so most statements are unanswered.

notes: Themes searched: economy, government, liberty, ecology, world and society statements against Hardin's 1968 essay, his Econlib entry, Britannica and the Gale entry. The sources speak only to population limits, coercive state powers, taxation and appeals to conscience. Hardin's later 'lifeboat ethics' are named by the sources only in a bibliography, so migration and aid are unanswered. Critics (Ostrom) were not used for answers.
